MATH2040 Linear Algebra II

Vector Space

A vector space over field $F$ is a set $V$ equipped with $+$ and $\times$, satisfying the axioms.

A subspace $W$ of vector space $V/F$ is a non-empty set where its closed under $+$ and $\times$.

Linear Independent, Span and Basis

Given a vector space $V$ and a set $S \subset V$. A vector $v$ is a linear combination of vectors in $S$, or in the span of $S$, $\langle S \rangle$, iff $$ v = a_1 \cdot u_1 + \cdots + a_n \cdot u_n $$ for some $a_i \in F$, $u_i \in V$. A relevant definition is that a set is linear independent iff we can only represent $0$ in one way, i.e., $$ 0 = a_1 \cdot u_1 + \cdots + a_n \cdot u_n \implies a_1 = \cdots = a_n = 0 $$ A set $S$ is a basis of $V$ if it is both linearly independent and spans $V$. The dimension of the vector space is defined to be the cardinality of its basis. A basis is guaranteed by Zorn's lemma, and all should have the same cardinality.

Operations on Vector Space

The sum of two subspaces $U$ and $W$ is defined to be $$ U + W = \{ u + w : u \in U, v \in W \} $$ If $ U \cap W = \{ 0 \} $, then it is called direct sum and is denoted $ U \oplus W $. Obviously $\dim (U \oplus W) = \dim (U) + \dim (W)$.

With this, we can define a projection operator $P : V \rightarrow U$ on $V = U \oplus W$ by mapping $u + w \in V$ to $u \in U$.

Similarly, the direct (cartesian) product of two vector spaces is defined by $$U \times W = \{ (u, w) : u \in U, w \in W \} $$

Quotient Space $V / W$ is defined on cosets $v + W$ for $v \in V$ under the same operators.

Linear Transformation

A linear transformation $T : V \rightarrow W$ is a map satisfying $T(v + w) = T(v) + T(w)$ and $T(av) = aT(v)$ for all $a \in F, v \in V, w \in W$.

The null space (kernel) of $T$ is defined as $$ \mathcal{N}(T) = \{ v: T(v) = 0 \} $$ Whereas the range (image) is defined as $$ \mathcal{R}(T) = \{ T(v) : v \in V \} $$ Rank-Nullity Theorem states that $$ \dim \mathcal{N}(T) + \dim \mathcal{R}(T) = \dim V $$

Matrix Representation

We can encode linear transformations with matrices. Consider finite-dim $V$ and $W$ with ordered basis $ \beta = \{ v_1, \cdots, v_n \} $ and $ \gamma = \{ w_1, \cdots, w_m \} $.

For vectors, say $v = a_1 v_1 + \cdots + a_n v_n$, then $$\phi_\beta(v) = [v]_\beta = (a_1, \cdots, a_n)^T$$ While for linear transformation $ T : V \rightarrow W $, we write $$ \Phi_{\beta, \gamma}(T) = [T]_\beta^\gamma = ( [Tv_1]_\gamma | \cdots | [Tv_n]_\gamma ) $$

Intuitively, we have $[T]_\beta^\gamma \cdot [U]_\alpha^\beta = [TU]_\alpha^\gamma$ and $[Tv]_\gamma = [T]_\beta^\gamma \cdot [v]_\beta$. For inverse linear map $T^{-1}$, we also have $ [T]_\beta \cdot [T^{-1}]_\beta = I $.

We can denote the space of linear transformation from $V$ to $W$ by $\mathcal{L}(V, W)$. The dual space is $V^* = \mathcal{L}(V, F)$, collection of linear functionals. If we define the dual map $T^* : W^* \rightarrow V^* $ to be $$ T^*(g) = g(T) \quad \forall g \in W^* $$ Then we have $ [T^*]_{\gamma^*}^{\beta^*} = ([T]_\beta^\gamma)^T$.

Finally, we can introduce the change of coordianates matrices. This is simply defined as $Q = [I_V]_\beta^\gamma$, which means $$ [T]_\beta = Q^{-1} \cdot [T]_\gamma \cdot Q$$ Two matrices are called similar iff there exists invertible $Q$ such that $$ B = Q^{-1} \cdot A \cdot Q $$
